# AI coding reliability guide

Use this guide before implementing or reviewing a change, especially a bug fix,
refactor, merge resolution or optimization. Its purpose is to turn recurring
failure modes into concrete design questions and executable checks. Compiling,
adding a timeout or passing a happy-path test does not establish reliability.

This guide owns the cross-cutting review method and reusable failure patterns.
[Module ownership](module-boundaries.md) owns implementation boundaries;
[architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md), [network contracts](network-design-reference.md)
and feature guides own behavior and resource limits. The
[testing workflow](testing-feedback-loop.md) owns commands, selection and gates.
Link to those owners instead of copying their changing contracts here. When code
and a contract disagree, resolve the intended behavior rather than documenting
the regression as the new rule.

## Use on every change

1. **Locate the owner and consumers.** Read the owning implementation, callers,
   existing tests and relevant guide before adding another helper or state owner.
   Include callbacks, IPC handlers, retries, startup, shutdown and recovery paths;
   an import graph alone cannot reveal all consumers.
2. **State the invariant and select risks.** Describe what must remain true on
   success, failure, cancellation and replacement. Use the table below to select
   applicable rules. A small diff can change lock order or lifetime semantics.
3. **Trace the failure path before editing.** For concurrency work, sketch who
   owns each lock, permit, task and mutable state; what it waits for; and who
   releases it. For a reproducible bug, construct a focused failing regression.
   Record unresolved hypotheses as hypotheses, not confirmed defects.
4. **Implement at the existing boundary.** Preserve authority, durable acceptance,
   compatibility and resource budgets. Recheck invariants after moving work
   outside a guard. Evaluate the proposed fix for new races and deadlocks too.
5. **Verify the changed boundary and report evidence.** Run affected checks and
   required boundary scenarios under the testing workflow. Explain results,
   exclusions and unresolved evidence. Update this guide when the defect exposes
   a reusable failure pattern; follow the maintenance procedure below.

Keep the risk explanation proportional to the change. A documentation edit does
not require a new concurrency test. A changed async callback does require a
lifetime review even when the diff is one line. Put task-specific reasoning and
results in the PR or ignored local evidence, not a new permanent report.

## Select rules by the changed boundary

| Change or symptom                                                        | Read at least                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Locks, callbacks, synchronous dispatch, UI freezes                       | [R01](#r01-lock-order-and-reentrant-calls), [R02](#r02-thread-and-scheduler-progress), [R10](#r10-evidence-that-exercises-the-failure)                |
| Background work, native providers, logout, shutdown or cancellation      | [R02](#r02-thread-and-scheduler-progress), [R03](#r03-actual-work-owns-its-lifetime), [R06](#r06-exact-authority-and-stale-completions)               |
| Network requests, retries, polling, queues or batches                    | [R03](#r03-actual-work-owns-its-lifetime), [R04](#r04-deadlines-cover-the-whole-operation), [R05](#r05-bounded-work-must-also-make-progress)          |
| React effects, IPC reads, dialogs, optimistic updates or mutation status | [R06](#r06-exact-authority-and-stale-completions), [R07](#r07-observation-is-not-mutation-ownership), [R10](#r10-evidence-that-exercises-the-failure) |
| Storage, settings, imports, deletion or recovery                         | [R06](#r06-exact-authority-and-stale-completions), [R08](#r08-durable-state-and-failure-semantics), [R09](#r09-bound-input-and-resource-use)          |
| IPC/API inputs, files, media or protocol changes                         | [R06](#r06-exact-authority-and-stale-completions), [R08](#r08-durable-state-and-failure-semantics), [R09](#r09-bound-input-and-resource-use)          |
| Merge resolution, shared helper or dependency changes                    | Revisit the affected callers and all applicable rules; a clean textual merge does not establish compatible ownership or semantics.                    |

These are starting points, not permission to ignore another reachable boundary.
Do not add a global lock, retry loop, timeout or shared abstraction solely to make
the local symptom disappear.

A frozen UI may result from a lock cycle, blocked event thread, starvation, lost
wakeup, unbounded work or stale loading state. Identify the mechanism and the
missing progress condition before selecting a fix; these need different evidence.

## R01: Lock order and reentrant calls

**Failure pattern:** one path takes A then B while another takes B then A; or a
helper/callback reacquires a nonrecursive lock its caller already holds. The
second case can deadlock on a single thread. Nested reads also need review when
a queued writer can prevent a new read from completing.

Trace actual acquisition order through callees, authorization callbacks,
destructors and error cleanup. Include main-thread dispatch and task joins as
wait dependencies, not just mutexes. A typical UI cycle is:

```text
background task: holds session guard -> waits for main-thread callback
main thread:     handles UI event    -> waits for session guard
```

Use the owning module's order; do not invent one universal order for unrelated
subsystems. Make whether a helper acquires a guard or requires one explicit.
Account archive snapshots, history projections and delivery recovery share the
plaintext-sidecar order: sent, received, then received files. Recovery must not
hold received while waiting for sent: an archive has no delivery guard and can
otherwise hold sent while waiting for received. The real recovery regression
`recovery_does_not_hold_received_while_waiting_for_sent` in the
[recovery owner](../crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/delivery_runtime.rs) holds sent,
probes received at the actual acquisition boundary, then releases contention and
joins the worker before asserting replay and progress.
Archive revision snapshots must read and release device-sync policy before
acquiring plaintext sidecars. Attachment commit holds delivery and policy while
checking the live received-file card; an archive holding received files while
waiting for policy creates a cycle and can also block erasure behind delivery.
Keep archive-key revalidation after indexing and page selection so a changed
policy still invalidates the export. The regression belongs to the
[account archive owner](../crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/account_sync/archive.rs)
and must qualify progress while the competing policy/sidecar boundary is held,
then release and join both owners before asserting the outcome.
The same boundary applies to file-proof revisions: identity import holds the
proof store while validating received-file rows. Archive snapshots must read and
release proof metadata before taking sidecars, and retain proof revision in the
final archive-key validation. Its separate held-proof regression qualifies the
actual archive path; policy-only coverage does not establish this lock order.
Do not build a revision array from chained mutex temporaries: guards can survive
until the entire array statement ends. Snapshot each value in a completed
statement before acquiring the next metadata lock. The archive's held-identity
control must also prove suppression is free, preserving the identity-then-
suppression order used by file-row visibility checks.
Avoid invoking arbitrary callbacks while guarded. Where a commit callback must
run inside an authority guard, keep that contract narrow and inspect its complete
call chain. Queue presentation without retaining a guard needed by the UI;
validate captured authority when the queued callback executes.

**Evidence:** exercise both competing paths and the real authorization variant.
An ordinary admission fixture does not cover a sensitive proof that itself locks
app state. Assert that the other operation progresses, not just that the first
eventually returns. See `checked_at_lock_revision` in
[runtime admission](../src-tauri/src/runtime_admission.rs), the verified-login
regression in [shared login tests](../src-tauri/src/shared_account_login/tests.rs),
and queued notification tests in [runtime state](../src-tauri/src/chat_commands/state.rs).

## R02: Thread and scheduler progress

**Failure pattern:** an `async` function performs blocking disk, crypto, OS-provider
or process work; a blocking worker retains a globally needed guard; or the parent
scheduler awaits optional work before polling unrelated ready operations.

Identify the executing thread and scheduling owner, not just the function's
signature. Move blocking work through the existing admitted worker boundary.
Inspect React render/effect/subscriber feedback loops and large synchronous data
transforms too; moving I/O off the UI thread does not bound those CPU costs.
Prepare bulk data outside shared commit guards, then reacquire the required
guards and revalidate before atomic publication. Keep critical sections small
without splitting a transaction or permitting stale side effects. Replacing a
mutex with an async mutex alone does not repair ownership or lock order.

Check that the UI event loop, accept loop and control scheduler can still make
progress while the worker is paused. Offloading a scan does not help other
branches of a scheduler if that scheduler still waits for the entire scan inside
one completion branch. Synchronous final persistence can still block; document
that boundary instead of claiming a timer can preempt it.

Branches of one `select!` share a task; adding runtime workers does not let a
blocked branch poll another branch of that same future. Independently scheduled
work must keep an explicit parent cancellation owner and retain the actual
child's retirement permit. The [inbound serving owner](../crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/serving.rs)
is exercised by the real maintenance-hold Noise regression in
[account action tests](../crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/account_group/tests/message_action_reference.rs),
alongside stalled-handshake retirement and the single-worker negative control.
Custom protocol and failed-initial-custody recovery fixtures must retain that
same independent host and retirement owner, including separate reactors for both
full-host participants and the synchronous history observer. The single-participant
connection-limit/retirement fixture likewise uses the production two-worker host;
retain its seven-slot saturation, original admission/retirement bounds and actual
socket closure checks, alongside the held-worker positive and single-thread
negative controls. This qualifies fixture capacity without attributing every
historical late admission to scheduler starvation. A source's synchronous durable append must not run on the receiver's
reactor. The growing-history regression in
[account sync tests](../crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/account_sync/selection_tests.rs)
holds the actual source writer until a receiver page imports, then measures
continuation progress separately from setup and checks advancing cursors.
Full-host file fixtures retain a separate two-worker reactor for each simulated
application. The [linked reconnect fixture](../crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/node_tests.rs)
also uses that owner at its original offline/online cuts and joins admitted work
before reopening a profile, on failure as well as success. This separates device
accept and maintenance loops; direct observer queries and public sends, including
caller-owned idle-expiry tasks, can still run on the observer reactor. A timer on
that reactor cannot bound a synchronous stall. Preserve the observation budget
and do not infer a particular deadlock or complete watchdog independence from an
unpolled timer alone. This includes the explicit account File result/retry rigs: use the
existing independent peer owner for source, requester, recipient and the launched
fresh sibling, keeping inactive retry phases and every byte/manifest assertion.
Release fault helpers before joining hosts, and preserve body failure after
actual retirement. Each online sender needs its normal delivery recovery owner
and an advertised address bound to its real listener. Local acceptance followed
by one best-effort flush cannot prove recovery after a transient exchange failure.
The [fresh-handshake and own-copy controls](../crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/delivery_runtime_tests.rs)
exercise recovery of the same accepted message without resending; the latter
holds both sibling workers after its durable copy completes and requires target
confirmation while they remain held; unrelated devices cannot share that stall.

**Evidence:** pause actual expensive work after admission and assert availability
of the unrelated guard or operation. Release the pause and verify the final data.
See the attachment preparation and document-scheduler regressions in
[account sync tests](../crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/account_sync/selection_tests.rs).

Async discovery observers must use the existing owned asynchronous peer-cache
snapshot and preserve persistence errors. The synchronous desktop convenience
snapshot writes storage and converts errors to an empty roster; polling it can
block the observer's reactor or misreport failed persistence as discovery latency.
The [account-login fixture](../src-tauri/src/shared_account_login/tests.rs) retains
its single signed loopback probe and original deadline, and a real cache-path
failure must preserve the cache API's error chain rather than time out. This
control proves error visibility, not the cause of an earlier hosted timeout.

## R03: Actual work owns its lifetime

Consume the canonical process owner's result contract rather than deriving a new
verdict from a diagnostic flag. Windows atomically terminates its owned job even
when empty, so verified `forcedRetirement` alone does not mean work leaked or a
successful test failed. Preserve the actual exit status and error, cancellation,
timeout and cleanup-verification results. The empty-job owner control and UI
runner outcome controls exercise that distinction.

Keep cancellation attached through owned log finalization. After command
closure, cancel unfinished log publication through the stream owner; partial
logs fail independently of the original exit status. Still join process-group
cleanup or verify the helper receipt: log closure cannot certify retirement.

POSIX process-group retirement proves only that group. A browser framework may
launch its web server in another group; use the actual tool's teardown protocol
and retain independent server-retirement controls in the UI command owner. Missing
cooperative teardown evidence cannot become verified cleanup merely because the
CLI exited or its group disappeared.
Tools such as Nextest and cargo-mutants create independently grouped children.
Killing their supervisor can close captured output while a real test remains
alive. Trace the tool's actual child ownership and shutdown protocol; neither
pipe closure nor the original group's disappearance proves retirement. The
[Linux mutation owner](../scripts/release/mutation-process-owner.py) uses a kernel
subreaper, pidfd-verified direct-child authority and one reaping loop across
normal exit and cancellation. If descriptor allocation fails, only a sole reaper
may signal a kernel-verified direct child whose status remains unreaped; consuming
that status before signalling would lose the identity guarantee. Child enumeration supplies candidates, not absence
proof; only kernel `ECHILD` after reaping establishes no owned descendants.
Missing, invalid or incomplete retirement acknowledgment keeps cleanup unverified.
Reserve the owner's bounded teardown window without changing ordinary callers'
defaults or using process names, stale PIDs or broad group sweeps as authority.
Actual direct-tool, nested-tool and active-build cancellation controls retain an
unrelated sibling and require acknowledged test retirement before returning.

Leader exit and output-pipe closure are separate lifecycle events. Bound draining
after owned-group retirement: an escaped descendant can retain inherited pipes
forever. Close only the owner's read ends, retain unverified cleanup and quarantine
its lease; the real detached-pipe natural-exit and cancellation controls exercise
this failure in the validation process owner.
Cleanup uncertainty is monotonic across cancellation and draining: successfully
retiring one group cannot clear an earlier unverified escaped-process boundary.
Retain the first failure while still awaiting every known retirement owner.

**Failure pattern:** cancelling an awaiter releases serialization or capacity while
its blocking worker, process or native provider continues; retries overlap, old
work writes into a new session, or shutdown waits for a worker while holding a
guard that worker needs to finish.

Name the owner of every task, timer, listener, subprocess, socket and permit.
Transfer required ownership into the actual work. Dropping an observer or timing
out a future is not evidence that external side effects stopped. Retain mutation
serialization and cleanup responsibility until real completion; bound admission
so repeated user retries cannot accumulate detached work.

A permit declared inside a blocking closure drops before the closure's remaining
captures. When those captures retain Node or storage handles, waking retirement
at that point can make close-before-reopen fail. Use the existing blocking work
owner in [runtime work](../crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/runtime_work.rs) for
[file/media maintenance](../crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/participant_runtime.rs),
so captures and undelivered results are destroyed before admission is released.
Keep the direct capture-drop ordering regression, queued cancellation and
undelivered-output controls, and the real native observer Node-release assertion;
do not narrow that assertion to conceal another producer retaining the profile.

A same-profile restart fixture must consume the existing retired storage close
before constructing its replacement. Joining producers through `stop()` alone
is not the fixture's proof that all Node and storage handles have closed. Keep
`stop_for_storage().await.close()` failure visible, including retained-handle
rejection, and preserve the subsequent durable reopen assertions. The shared
settings projection/restart scenario exercises this boundary with its old weak
application token still present; do not replace closure with a sleep or remove
the restart tail.

Follow the existing retirement protocol: close admission, signal cancellation,
release guards needed for completion, join owned tasks and drain admitted work.
Uncancellable native work needs an explicit ownership boundary: retain the
operation's serialization ownership, but not unrelated runtime/session guards across
the provider call. Reval…6343 tokens truncated…cument category and entitlement
checks still apply. Together with control and directory work, these remain four
workers in the same shared session pool, not additional network capacity.

### Account profiles and private trust

`identity/account.rs` and `identity/account_keystore.rs` own immutable creation
metadata persisted with the account key. Pairing and recovery preserve it without
inferring missing dates. `node/account_profile_data.rs` owns signed bounded
ordinary profile data and current-profile persistence; `node/account_profile_io.rs`
owns admitted edits, authenticated reception and legacy compatibility.
`node/profile_receive_work.rs` owns account-scoped exact receive evidence and
retry scheduling on the profile's encrypted SQL connection. Discovery advances
through at most 128 committed event headers; each retry pass selects 16 fixed
metadata rows before loading one signed body at a time. Unknown devices and
disabled sibling-profile synchronization remain pending. Current-profile writes
finish before processed evidence is committed, so a crash or storage failure
retries idempotently. No historical profile-ID set is rebuilt in memory.
Send preparation enters host authority before acquiring the delivery journal.
Desktop biography saves reply after durable local acceptance while admitted fanout
continues independently. The ordinary nickname and bio edit share the publication
mutex, preventing a stale bio save from undoing a rename.
Profile-store guards end before delivery preparation acquires channel, routing or
event-log state. Group inventory first snapshots channel facts, releases the channel
book, then resolves profile names and routing classifications. Neither side may
retain one of these guards while waiting for the other. Deterministic lock-boundary
regressions cover background publication, biography/avatar edits and inventory
projection; keep them in both affected validation selections.
`src-tauri/src/account_profile.rs` exposes reads and bio edits, with no caller-supplied
names, timestamps or public proofs. `src-tauri/src/trust.rs` owns private observation
history and manual verification. Frontend `store/accountProfiles.ts` shares
session-bound profile reads and live invalidations across the header and dialogs.
The [profile and verification guide](peer-trust.md) owns meanings and evidence limits.

## Google Drive recovery transport

`src-tauri/src/google_drive/` owns remembered password-encrypted local OAuth
refresh grants, ephemeral operation connections, exact-session admission, bounded
Drive HTTP transfers and temporary encrypted file lifetimes. Its `remembered.rs`
keeps Google credentials native and separate from recovery archives.
`src-tauri/src/recovery.rs` remains the owner of consistent snapshot/runtime restart,
archive verification and transactional profile restore. Its `recovery/setup.rs`
owns the reusable local recovery key, one-time acknowledgement and selected
destination, using the existing password-encrypted local-user storage and exact
session/lock authority. `core/recovery/` owns format
and cryptography. `ui/lib/api/googleDrive.ts` adapts IPC, and
`ui/features/recovery/` provides shared connection/progress presentation for the
existing export/restore dialogs. See [backup and recovery](backup-recovery.md#google-drive-security-and-boundaries).

## Bounded history for channel invitations

`channel/history.rs` owns the four fixed history policy presets. The existing
channel lifecycle in `node/channels.rs` owns invitations; `node/join_history.rs`
owns frozen encrypted copies, owner-policy validation and post-acceptance row-key
release. It reuses the delivery journal, channel crypto primitives, causal
membership projection and received-history store. Desktop IPC delegates authority
to core; the member dialog presents the policy without independently deciding
history eligibility. The [channel guide](help/topics/channels.md#history-for-new-members)
owns user-visible limits and availability.

Native message presentation is queued onto the UI thread before acquiring the
exact desktop-session guard. The queued callback revalidates its session and runtime
ticket before emitting private events or notifications. A worker must not hold that
guard while synchronously querying window focus: the UI thread may itself be waiting
for the same session. `events.rs` owns this dispatch boundary and its lock-order and
stale-session regressions; `runtime_bootstrap.rs` uses it for DM, group and file callbacks.

### Account document projections

`node/account_documents/` owns private typed metadata and blobs, not group
authority or public identity. The existing account worker and session carry
manifest pages and bounded chunks; there is no second network daemon. Native
`account_documents.rs` checks exact local owner, runtime account and version
before mutations or plaintext release. Frontend linked coordinators project
accepted records into the owning draft, reception, pack and avatar stores; they
never own another network synchronization loop. Pack validation remains in
`pack.ts`; pack storage is namespaced by local owner and cryptographic account.
`settings/shared.rs` owns the allowlist mapping of portable settings onto existing
per-key account preferences. Device paths, system permissions, autostart and
local-agent grants stay outside the replicated allowlist.
`account_documents/controls.rs` owns authenticated private DM control publication,
original-action ordering and sibling projections. `reactions.rs` and `recall.rs`
publish accepted actions through it; generic native document mutations cannot
create control records. Explicit kept-source preparation validates legacy caches.
`account_sync/archive.rs` filters known recalled private bodies/cards and invalidates cached
exports when the control revision changes. Group authority and local deletion
remain with their existing owners.

`channel_custody.rs` owns locally observed exact-event possession and retractions;
its indexed child keeps those exact positive and negative observations in the
leased profile database, with selected-event reads and 32-row keyset migration
pages. It shares the history-source publisher and legacy-writer barrier rather
than retaining the custody journal in memory. Auxiliary source identities 16–18
use a separate registry without rewriting the installed transcript-source schema.
`account_documents/custody.rs` owns their account-private versioned publication
and sibling projection. It reuses certified account sessions and document digests,
without adding a group transport or claiming recipient delivery. Channel authority
determines eligible external member principals. The footer distinguishes missing
status from a known zero count; its status coordinator clears stale projections
only for the messages and runtime lifetime it requested.
The document store keeps a separate bounded custody-key quota and an owned-file
scan budget consistent with legal document counts. `media_store.rs` prunes the
enumerated unreferenced regular files in one pass, preserving live files and
synchronizing the parent directory before successful return.

`account_documents/public_profile.rs` relays original signed contact profiles under
Profile consent; `account_profile_io.rs` retains signature, revision and avatar
projection authority. Per-source document heads preserve each contact's original
profile. Constructor work initializes only the optional reconciliation receipts;
the existing account-sync worker repairs at most sixteen publication heads and
sixteen projection heads per turn. Exact account/device-scoped completion receipts
compare accepted profile change revisions or signed document revision/hash before
loading avatars. Missing or failed receipts remain retryable after restart; an
unchanged warm open does not replay contact document payloads. Canonical profile
admission and its interrupted avatar projection keep their existing owners.
`account_documents/group_activity.rs` owns History-gated source-signed control
observations tied to the selected inventory snapshot. It cannot install membership
or keys. Both reuse the existing document worker and certified sibling sessions.

`account_documents/inventory.rs` owns source-certified descriptive group snapshots,
bounded automatic publication and account-private reference projection. It reuses
the document version/digest owner and private account worker. The group directory
is mandatory account topology; optional history, profile, appearance and contact
data retain their existing policies. A source reads real local group state and
never republishes a borrowed reference as authority. The native channel adapter
may project reference member facts for display under runtime admission; group
authorization, keys and mutations remain exclusively with the existing channel
owners. The frontend distinguishes this read-only reference from a backup archive
and removes its explanation when real validated group state arrives.


`node/account_documents/device_hostname.rs` owns bounded private per-device hostname
publication and certified-roster projection. The desktop runtime bootstrap reads
OS hostnames; admitted sync IPC releases them only for the expected current account.
`PersonalDevices` renders them without changing identity, account nicknames or
presence semantics. Hostnames reuse encrypted account-document persistence and the
existing certified sibling transport; public discovery and profiles never carry
them. See [private account synchronization](network-design-reference.md#g-linking-and-ongoing-account-synchronization).

name: systematic-debugging
description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
---

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultrathink this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

**Related skills:**
- **superpowers:test-driven-development** - For creating failing test case (Phase 4, Step 1)
- **superpowers:verification-before-completion** - Verify fix worked before claiming success

## Real-World Impact

From debugging sessions:
- Systematic approach: 15-30 minutes to fix
- Random fixes approach: 2-3 hours of thrashing
- First-time fix rate: 95% vs 40%
- New bugs introduced: Near zero vs common

# Keeping CI fast and reliable

Treat feedback time, reliability and resource use as maintained requirements.
Every feature, dependency and test can change CI cost, even without a workflow
edit. AI agents and contributors should preserve useful coverage while reducing
unnecessary work, and leave failures easier to reproduce and diagnose.

This guide owns CI maintenance decisions and regression prevention. It does not
introduce another workflow, command catalog or acceptance policy.

| Question                                            | Authoritative owner                                                                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Which tests, commands and CI jobs apply?            | [Testing feedback loop](testing-feedback-loop.md), owning `validation.json` contracts and [workflow definitions](../.github/workflows/) |
| What evidence permits acceptance or release?        | [Quality gates](quality-gates.md) and [version and release lifecycle](updates.md#version-ownership-and-lifecycle)                       |
| Where does an implementation or shared rule belong? | [Module ownership](module-boundaries.md) and [script entry points](../scripts/README.md)                                                |
| Which consumers and documentation need updating?    | [Change alignment checklist](maintenance-checklist.md) and [documentation guidelines](DOCUMENTATION_GUIDELINES.md)                      |

Keep tool versions, matrix sizes, deadlines, cache keys and required-check names
in their existing executable owners. Keep run histories and investigation output
in ignored `tmp/` or PR/CI artifacts; durable decisions belong in the owning guide.

## Make the cost of a change explicit

Before adding a suite, fixture, dependency, platform or workflow, identify the
existing owner and the observable failure it must detect. Inspect the affected
plan and consumers through the [validation protocol](testing-feedback-loop.md#validation-stages-and-agent-responsibilities).
Answer four questions in the change when they are material:

- What requirement needs new evidence, and why is existing evidence insufficient?
- Which layer and platform can exercise that requirement faithfully?
- What recurring setup, compilation, execution and artifact cost will it add?
- Can an existing task, fixture or compatible output supply it without weakening
  assertions or introducing another owner for the same rule?

Extend the existing implementation first. Share policy and lifecycle rules where
their meaning is identical; keep feature-specific fixtures local. An abstraction
is useful when it removes duplicated decisions and has clear inputs, outputs and
failure behavior. Avoid both copied shell fragments and a generic CI framework
whose configuration is harder to review than the work it coordinates.

Do not make a full local suite the default for every edit. Use affected feedback
while developing, then complete the applicable boundary and candidate gates.
New tests still need independent assertions; matching the implementation or
increasing a test count does not establish useful coverage.

## Keep workflow policy thin and reject cheap failures locally

Workflows own triggers, permissions, runners, matrices, dependencies and artifact
transport. Scripts own inventory validation, artifact roles, packaging, report
collection and execution policy. Reuse the same CLI locally and in Actions;
extract substantial conditionals and loops into the existing feature owner rather
than copying YAML fragments or introducing another generic orchestration layer.
When moving execution into a script, update every caller and smoke check. Keep
launcher behavior in its owning regression instead of requiring obsolete command
text in YAML. Cross-platform filesystem paths use `fileURLToPath` rather than
`.pathname`; ESM module arguments retain a file URL or relative module specifier
instead of a native Windows absolute path. Exercise each boundary on its platform.
Keep live source/release checks immediately before each publication boundary;
those protect against changed state and are not redundant setup checks.

Consolidate pure checks only when their immutable candidate, scope and inputs are
identical. Health's full-scope Linux portable job owns source standards and Git
index hygiene after frontend dependency setup; documentation scope retains its
independent source gate. Real checker portability fixtures still run on every
Health platform. Native CI alone supplies partial acceptance: the protected
current-source Health check in the UI workflow and the complete release source
check closure remain necessary. Keep checks at distinct candidate, artifact,
trust or runtime boundaries, including archive producer and consumer identity and
cleanliness checks. Removing repeated source invocations does not establish a
hosted speedup; measure runner cost and latency separately.

The [syntax owner](../scripts/validation/syntax.mjs) parses changed Node, Bash and
Python sources without executing them or writing Python caches, and invokes
`actionlint` for changed workflows. Pre-commit selects staged paths but checks
worktree bytes, matching the existing structural checks. Affected validation also
checks new nonignored sources; PR creation checks the clean committed comparison.
Use Node 22, Bash and Python; install actionlint before changing workflows. No
checker installs tools or contacts the network. Hook installation configures hooks
without launching comprehensive health; request that gate explicitly.
Run the configured spelling check on changed files before publication, and scan
the repository when its configuration changes. Scope unavoidable external API
spellings to their language and identifier; do not exclude a source tree or
replace the API name to satisfy a prose checker.

PR creation runs `make pr-check`'s cheap-check owner against its actual comparison
base, rejects ownership blockers and checks applicable frontend patch coverage
before publication. The creation wrapper accepts repeated `--owner ID` and
`--reason TEXT` before `--` and forwards them only to that existing affected-plan
owner. Review every otherwise unmapped path before making this explicit selection;
it records responsibility, not test acceptance. Platform selectors remain separate,
and missing/invalid owners, absent reasons and checker failures still block creation.
Version projections, contract references and hygiene already
belong to structural standards; reuse that owner rather than adding duplicate
gates. Do not install dependencies, compile Rust, launch browsers or run application suites
implicitly in the cheap mode. Source changes during checking invalidate it.
Workflow edits also run the existing fast CI policy owner locally. Configuration
assertions and runner inventory discovery belong here; application execution and
native compiler fixtures do not. Keep static policy assertions independently runnable
without native tool setup. Scope fixture configuration changes to their owning
table or profile; repeated valid values elsewhere must remain unchanged. Update the existing policy assertion when its
requirement changes instead of adding a second overlapping test in another file.
Write generated reports into the task-owned evidence directory, not the source
checkout. Fixtures for source-integrity checks must preserve production ignore
rules; adding a fixture-only ignore can hide a real dirty-worktree failure.
For entry-point changes, also run the affected contract tests selected by the
existing validation plan before publication. A syntax pass or a hand-picked
filename sample cannot detect stale semantic routing expectations; cheap PR
checks do not certify those tests passed.

The frontend precheck reads the target from `codecov.yml`, includes partially
covered branches in the uncovered denominator and rejects omitted changed files.
Exercise report readers against actual producer output as well as small fixtures;
negative V8 branch counts remain uncovered rather than invalidating the report.
It verifies an existing clean-candidate `frontend-coverage` receipt through the
canonical stage owner and rechecks LCOV bytes, rather than trusting a timestamp or
raw report. Generate missing evidence explicitly with the reported command. A
verification-only miss never starts coverage, waits for a heavy lock or claims a
pass; a no-work verification lease must not imply admitted child work. Keep
verified scope termination diagnostics separate from the actual test result.
This frontend unit precheck is conservative; Rust and browser-union coverage
still need their owning evidence. Native execution, dependency resolution and
published-asset verification cannot be replaced by parsing or stale build output.

Use the existing package inventory's `frontendBuild` ownership when preparing
Rust selectors. Core, integrations and MCP selections still require real target
# Mesh-Talk Architecture

A decentralized, end-to-end-encrypted messenger. **Tauri** desktop shell, **Rust**
backend, **React + TypeScript** frontend. No vendor-operated server: LAN peers
discover each other over signed UDP **multicast** (group `224.0.0.167`, port
47474), connect directly over a Noise-encrypted TCP
channel, and store messages as an append-only, hash-linked **event log** that syncs CRDT-style.
When a peer is offline, a peer-operated **post office** node stores-and-forwards the (still-encrypted)
events. Existing routed networks can supply optional peer discovery; opted-in
post-office bridges introduce registered peers across sites without merging
their IP subnets. See [routed discovery](routed-network-discovery.md) and
[Network Topology and Communication Architecture](network-design-reference.md)
for cross-module design contracts, illustrated scenarios and development guardrails;
[network topologies](network-topologies.md) provides the compact overview.

> The earlier RSA-contact / plaintext-UDP / TCP-relay _legacy_ stack has been retired;
> this local-first stack is the entire product and lives at `/`. The only retained
> piece outside the node is the auth/session layer (`services/auth_service.rs` + `state.rs`),
> which `login` uses before starting the node.

---

Use the [canonical domain glossary](../CONTEXT.md) and
[DDD conventions](domain-design.md) for terminology and identifier translations.
This reference owns technical mechanisms and invariants.

## 1. Process & layers

See the [module ownership and reuse guide](module-boundaries.md) before assigning
parallel feature work or adding shared business logic. It maps current owners and
feature-local interfaces across the core, desktop host and frontend.

```
React UI ── lib/api/*.ts ──invoke()──▶ Tauri IPC (chat_commands/)
   ▲                                    │
   │ Tauri events                       ▼
   └─────────────── RuntimeEvents ← NodeRuntime (node/runtime.rs)
                                           │ discovery, accept, maintenance
                                           ▼
                                   Node (node/node.rs) — orchestration
        ┌──────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┬───────┴──────┐
   identity/      transport/        eventlog/       discovery/    postoffice/
   ratchet/       (Noise XX)        (DAG + sync)    (signed UDP)  (elect+relay)
   channel/ dm/
        └────────────── storage/encryption.rs (PBKDF2-600k + AES-256-GCM at rest) ──┘
```

`mesh-talk-core` owns protocol state, network tasks, and encrypted persistence.
The desktop shell composes it using `RuntimeConfig` and `RuntimeEvents` in
`src-tauri/src/commands.rs`. `NodeRuntime::start` remains a compatibility
constructor for SDK callers. The shell owns the session and translates inbound
events to Tauri events; it does not own protocol or wire types. Desktop IPC
commands live in `src-tauri/src/chat_commands/`, grouped by account, messaging,
channels, files, platform, and diagnostics. `mod.rs` re-exports the established
command names for Tauri registration. Sensitive IPC commands capture `RuntimeAdmission` before waiting on `NodeState`.
Blocking operations retain runtime lifecycle and matching session authority until
completion, even when their IPC waiter is cancelled. Asynchronous producers use
guarded core commit seams; plaintext queries recheck the originating admission
before returning results. A cloned node handle alone conveys no session authority.
The installed runtime slot uses shared operation leases and exclusive replacement
access. Network waits in one producer must not serialize identity, presence,
history or unrelated sends. Retirement still waits for every admitted lease;
session authorization continues to enclose synchronous commits.

## 2. Crypto & identity (`identity/`, `transport/`, `ratchet/`, `dm/`, `channel/`)

### Protected messages

Text and image messages can carry an authenticated `MessageProtection` policy: explicit
click-to-view, or authentication with the viewing device's existing app-lock
mechanism. Core history, search and received-event projections omit protected
content; explicit exact-message text and image queries are available to authorized
hosts. Ordinary image read and export APIs reject protected images.
The encrypted sent/received stores and eligible history replication retain the
full protected body. Ordinary text/reply and sticker wire layouts stay unchanged.
#[tauri::command]
pub async fn create_channel(
    app: tauri::State<'_, AppState>,
    state: tauri::State<'_, NodeState>,
    name: String,
    member_account_ids: Vec<String>,
) -> Result<String, CommandError> {
    let admission = RuntimeAdmission::capture_current(&app, &state)?;
    admission
        .detached(move |runtime, admission| {
            Box::pin(async move {
                let node = admission.checked(runtime, || Ok(runtime.handle()))?;
                let id = node
                    .create_account_channel_invited_if(&name, member_account_ids, |commit| {
                        admission.authorize_accept(runtime, commit)
                    })
                    .await
                    .map_err(CommandError::from)?;
                Ok(hex::encode(id.as_bytes()))
            })
        })
        .await
}

# Mesh-Talk Architecture

A decentralized, end-to-end-encrypted messenger. **Tauri** desktop shell, **Rust**
backend, **React + TypeScript** frontend. No vendor-operated server: LAN peers
discover each other over signed UDP **multicast** (group `224.0.0.167`, port
47474), connect directly over a Noise-encrypted TCP
channel, and store messages as an append-only, hash-linked **event log** that syncs CRDT-style.
When a peer is offline, a peer-operated **post office** node stores-and-forwards the (still-encrypted)
events. Existing routed networks can supply optional peer discovery; opted-in
post-office bridges introduce registered peers across sites without merging
their IP subnets. See [routed discovery](routed-network-discovery.md) and
[Network Topology and Communication Architecture](network-design-reference.md)
for cross-module design contracts, illustrated scenarios and development guardrails;
[network topologies](network-topologies.md) provides the compact overview.

> The earlier RSA-contact / plaintext-UDP / TCP-relay _legacy_ stack has been retired;
> this local-first stack is the entire product and lives at `/`. The only retained
> piece outside the node is the auth/session layer (`services/auth_service.rs` + `state.rs`),
> which `login` uses before starting the node.

---

Use the [canonical domain glossary](../CONTEXT.md) and
[DDD conventions](domain-design.md) for terminology and identifier translations.
This reference owns technical mechanisms and invariants.

## 1. Process & layers

See the [module ownership and reuse guide](module-boundaries.md) before assigning
parallel feature work or adding shared business logic. It maps current owners and
feature-local interfaces across the core, desktop host and frontend.

```
React UI ── lib/api/*.ts ──invoke()──▶ Tauri IPC (chat_commands/)
   ▲                                    │
   │ Tauri events                       ▼
   └─────────────── RuntimeEvents ← NodeRuntime (node/runtime.rs)
                                           │ discovery, accept, maintenance
                                           ▼
                                   Node (node/node.rs) — orchestration
        ┌──────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┬───────┴──────┐
   identity/      transport/        eventlog/       discovery/    postoffice/
   ratchet/       (Noise XX)        (DAG + sync)    (signed UDP)  (elect+relay)
   channel/ dm/
        └────────────── storage/encryption.rs (PBKDF2-600k + AES-256-GCM at rest) ──┘
```

`mesh-talk-core` owns protocol state, network tasks, and encrypted persistence.
The desktop shell composes it using `RuntimeConfig` and `RuntimeEvents` in
`src-tauri/src/commands.rs`. `NodeRuntime::start` remains a compatibility
constructor for SDK callers. The shell owns the session and translates inbound
events to Tauri events; it does not own protocol or wire types. Desktop IPC
commands live in `src-tauri/src/chat_commands/`, grouped by account, messaging,
channels, files, platform, and diagnostics. `mod.rs` re-exports the established
command names for Tauri registration. Sensitive IPC commands capture `RuntimeAdmission` before waiting on `NodeState`.
Blocking operations retain runtime lifecycle and matching session authority until
completion, even when their IPC waiter is cancelled. Asynchronous producers use
guarded core commit seams; plaintext queries recheck the originating admission
before returning results. A cloned node handle alone conveys no session authority.
The installed runtime slot uses shared operation leases and exclusive replacement
access. Network waits in one producer must not serialize identity, presence,
history or unrelated sends. Retirement still waits for every admitted lease;
session authorization continues to enclose synchronous commits.

## 2. Crypto & identity (`identity/`, `transport/`, `ratchet/`, `dm/`, `channel/`)

### Protected messages

Text and image messages can carry an authenticated `MessageProtection` policy: explicit
click-to-view, or authentication with the viewing device's existing app-lock
mechanism. Core history, search and received-event projections omit protected
content; explicit exact-message text and image queries are available to authorized
hosts. Ordinary image read and export APIs reject protected images.
The encrypted sent/received stores and eligible history replication retain the
full protected body. Ordinary text/reply and sticker wire layouts stay unchanged.
#[tauri::command]
pub async fn create_channel(
    app: tauri::State<'_, AppState>,
    state: tauri::State<'_, NodeState>,
    name: String,
    member_account_ids: Vec<String>,
) -> Result<String, CommandError> {
    let admission = RuntimeAdmission::capture_current(&app, &state)?;
    admission
        .detached(move |runtime, admission| {
            Box::pin(async move {
                let node = admission.checked(runtime, || Ok(runtime.handle()))?;
                let id = node
                    .create_account_channel_invited_if(&name, member_account_ids, |commit| {
                        admission.authorize_accept(runtime, commit)
                    })
                    .await
                    .map_err(CommandError::from)?;
                Ok(hex::encode(id.as_bytes()))
            })
        })
        .await
}
